quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on capacity, set-up, efficiency, double passes and bottlenecks in a finishing plant.

questions.q: In the lecture, the calculated efficiency of a continuous machine is:
questions.explain: For a 10,000 m run: 200 ÷ (200 + 90) = 69.0%. Set-up time is the share of the clock that produces nothing.

questions.q: What makes up the 90 minutes of set-up per run on the thermosol range?
options: Cleaning 30 min and preparation and matching 60 min
Ten per cent of the run time
questions.explain: The sheet enters average cleaning of 30 min and average preparation and shade matching of 60 min, totalling 90 min for each run.

questions.q: Net efficiency is the calculated efficiency less the miscellaneous losses, taken as 10 percentage points.
questions.explain: 69.0% − 10% = 59.0%. The miscellaneous allowance covers stoppages that the set-up figures do not capture.

questions.q: A machine that must pass the fabric twice (for example dye then wash on the same range) has, for that fabric:
options: Capacity reduced by the set-up time only
questions.explain: Each metre occupies the machine twice, so the metres of finished fabric per day are halved; the sheet adjusts by dividing by (1 + share of double pass).

questions.q: The overall capacity of the plant is set by:
options: The average of all machine capacities
questions.explain: Fabric cannot leave faster than the slowest stage it must pass; the lecture identifies thermosol and stenter dyeing, at 34,000 m a day each, as the lines to watch.

questions.q: Which machines does the lecture call "the lines to watch"?
questions.explain: Both are limited to about 34,000 m a day after double passes, far below the 126,000 m plant balance, so any shift of the mix towards them creates a bottleneck.

questions.q: Mercerizing shows 57,600 m/day for the machine but 155,520 m/day "overall". Why is the overall figure larger?
options: Only 50/135 of the plant's fabric is mercerized
questions.explain: If only 50 of every 135 m need mercerizing, 57,600 m of mercerizing supports 57,600 × 135 ÷ 50 = 155,520 m of total plant output.

questions.q: On the printing machine, a colour change takes less set-up time than a design change.
questions.explain: The notes give set-up of 60 min on average, less for a colour change and more for a design change, because a design change means changing the screens.

questions.q: Why are the two finishing stenters' 207,360 m/day divided by 2.25?
options: Because all non-stenter-dyed fabric passes twice and some passes a third time after mercerizing
Because efficiency is 80% and losses are 10%
questions.explain: A double pass for setting and finishing counts 2, and the occasional extra pass after mercerizing adds a quarter, giving 207,360 ÷ 2.25 = 92,160 m.

questions.q: The minimum run the lecture allows on the thermosol range is:
questions.explain: Below 3,000 yd the 90-minute set-up swamps the run time and efficiency collapses; 10,000 m is the proposed run size used for the capacity calculation.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The capacity formula and what happens to it when run size, set-up, speed or double passes change.

questions.q: Capacity of a machine in metres per day is:
options: Speed × 1,440 × net efficiency × number of machines
Run size × runs per day ÷ set-up
questions.explain: 50 m/min × 1,440 min × 0.59 × 1 machine = 42,455 m a day. Dividing by efficiency would wrongly enlarge the capacity.

questions.q: If the run size doubles with the same set-up time, the calculated efficiency:
questions.explain: A 20,000 m run takes 400 min: 400 ÷ (400 + 90) = 81.6% against 69.0%, because the same 90 minutes of set-up is spread over twice the run.

questions.q: Longer preparation and matching time, with the run unchanged, means:
options: No change in efficiency, only in speed
questions.explain: Set-up time is in the denominator of run ÷ (run + set-up); more of it lowers efficiency and so capacity.

questions.q: A 10,000 m run at 50 m/min takes 200 minutes of production time.
questions.explain: Run time = run size ÷ speed = 10,000 ÷ 50 = 200 min, before any set-up.

questions.q: Capacity adjusted for double pass is found by:
options: Dividing capacity by (1 + share needing a double pass)
Multiplying capacity by (1 + share needing a double pass)
Halving the capacity whatever the share
questions.explain: With 25% needing a second pass, 42,455 ÷ 1.25 = 33,964 m a day. Halving would only be right if every metre passed twice.

questions.q: If every metre of fabric on a range needed a double pass, its adjusted capacity would be:
options: Three quarters of the single-pass capacity
questions.explain: Dividing by (1 + 1.00) = 2 halves the capacity, as the lecture says for a double thermosol or dye + wash.

questions.q: A process is needed by only a fraction f of the plant's fabric. The plant output that one machine supports is:
questions.explain: Calendering handles 80,640 m a day; with 40% of fabric calendered, overall = 80,640 ÷ 0.40 = 201,600 m.

questions.q: Miscellaneous losses are subtracted as percentage points, so a 69% calculated efficiency becomes 59%, not 62.1%.
questions.explain: The sheet computes B7 − B8 = 69% − 10% = 59%. Multiplying 69% × 90% = 62.1% is a common error that overstates capacity.

questions.q: The factor 1,440 in the capacity formula is:
questions.explain: 24 hours × 60 minutes = 1,440 minutes; metres per minute × minutes per day gives metres per day.

questions.q: For the thermosol range (10,000 m runs, 50 m/min, 90 min set-up, 10% losses), which change raises daily capacity the most?
options: Raising speed to 60 m/min with the same run
Doubling the run size to 20,000 m
questions.explain: Doubling the run gives 72,000 × (400 ÷ 490 − 0.10) = 51,575 m. Speed 60 m/min gives about 47,460 m (the shorter run lowers efficiency); 5% losses give 46,055 m; more cleaning lowers capacity.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute run times, efficiencies and daily capacities for the machines in the lecture's plant.

questions.q: A run of 10,000 m on a range running at 50 m/min: production time for the run, in minutes?
Run time is 200 min; cleaning 30 min and preparation and matching 60 min per run. Calculated efficiency, in % to one decimal?
Calculated efficiency is 69.0% and miscellaneous losses are 10 percentage points. Net efficiency, in %?
One thermosol range at 50 m/min, 24 hours a day, net efficiency 59.0% (exactly 200/290 − 0.10). Capacity in metres per day, to the nearest 10 m?
Capacity is 42,455 m/day and 25% of the fabric needs a double pass. Capacity adjusted for double pass, to the nearest 10 m?
The bleaching range runs at 120 m/min at 80% efficiency, 24 hours a day. Capacity in metres per day?
Pad steam: 10,000 m runs at 70 m/min, set-up 70 min per run, miscellaneous losses 10 points. Capacity in metres per day, to the nearest 10 m?
Two finishing stenters at 90 m/min and 80% efficiency; fabric needs 2.25 passes on average. Usable finishing capacity in metres per day?
questions.explain: 2 × 90 × 1,440 × 0.80 = 207,360 m of passes; ÷ 2.25 = 92,160 m of finished fabric.

questions.q: The calender runs 70 m/min at 80% efficiency and only 40% of the plant's fabric is calendered. What plant output per day does it support?
questions.explain: Machine capacity 80,640 m; ÷ 0.40 = 201,600 m of total plant output.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning decisions in a finishing plant: minimum runs, shifting load, changeovers and the bottleneck.

questions.q: Sales wants to accept 2,000 yd lots for thermosol dyeing. The planning office resists because:
options: The dyes will not fix on short lengths
The lot is below the 3,000 yd minimum: 90 min of set-up against a short run collapses efficiency
Short lots need a double pass
The range cannot be stopped between lots
questions.explain: 2,000 yd is about 1,829 m, a 37-minute run; efficiency = 37 ÷ 127 = 29% before losses, so the range would spend most of its day cleaning and matching.

questions.q: Thermosol is limiting output at 34,000 m a day. Which action raises the plant's dyeing capacity?
options: Shift fabrics that need the dye + wash double pass to the pad steam range when it has spare capacity
Run shorter lots to serve more customers
Add cleaning time to improve quality
questions.explain: Pad steam dyes and washes in one pass and has 46,000 m of capacity; moving double-pass work there frees thermosol time. The other options lower or do not touch dyeing capacity.

questions.q: Because only 50/135 of the fabric is mercerized, one mercerizer with 57,600 m/day supports a plant output of 155,520 m/day.
questions.explain: 57,600 × 135 ÷ 50 = 155,520 m, comfortably above the plant's 126,000 m balance, so mercerizing is not the bottleneck.

questions.q: The printing planner groups all colourways of one design together before moving to the next design. The reason is:
options: Colour changes are cheaper in dyes
A colour change needs less set-up than a design change, so set-up time per run falls
Designs must be printed in catalogue order
questions.explain: Average set-up is 60 min, less for a colour change and more for a design change (new screens). Grouping colourways keeps most changeovers as the cheap kind.

questions.q: The plant has promised buyers 126,000 m a day. The order mix then shifts towards dark shades dyed on the thermosol range. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; the plant is balanced at 126,000 m
Thermosol becomes the bottleneck at about 34,000 m and deliveries slip
questions.explain: The 126,000 m balance assumes the mix spread across continuous, batch, stenter dyeing and printing. If thermosol work exceeds 34,000 m a day, the rest of the plant waits.

questions.q: Cleaning time on thermosol is cut from 30 to 15 minutes per 10,000 m run (speed 50 m/min, matching 60 min, losses 10 points). Daily capacity becomes about:
A machine's calculated efficiency can be raised simply by scheduling longer runs of the same shade.
questions.explain: Longer runs spread the fixed set-up over more metres: 20,000 m runs give 81.6% instead of 69.0% on the thermosol range.

questions.q: Sanforizing supports 161,280 m/day when 50% of fabric is sanforized. Buyers now want 80% of the fabric sanforized. The result is:
options: Sanforizing supports 100,800 m/day and becomes the bottleneck below the plant's 126,000 m
No change, because machine capacity is still 80,640 m
questions.explain: 80,640 ÷ 0.80 = 100,800 m of plant output, less than 126,000 m, so the sanforizer now limits the plant. A second machine or a second shift pattern would be needed.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT counted inside the set-up time in the thermosol example?
questions.explain: Set-up = cleaning 30 + preparation and matching 60 = 90 min. The miscellaneous 10 points are deducted separately from the calculated efficiency.

questions.q: Stenter-dyed fabric does not need the double pass on the finishing stenters. What does that imply for planning?
options: Routing more fabric through stenter dyeing lightens the load on the finishing stenters
The finishing stenters must run slower
questions.explain: The 2.25-pass divisor applies to non-stenter-dyed fabric; stenter-dyed fabric is finished as it is dyed, so each metre routed that way saves two finishing passes.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder, two-step capacity questions and the common mistakes in efficiency arithmetic.

questions.q: Thermosol: 5,000 m runs at 50 m/min, set-up 90 min, miscellaneous losses 10 points, one machine. Capacity in metres per day, to the nearest 10 m?
questions.explain: Run = 100 min; efficiency = 100 ÷ 190 = 52.6%; net 42.6%; 72,000 × 0.426 = 30,695 m, far below the 42,455 m with 10,000 m runs.

questions.q: Doubling the thermosol run from 10,000 m to 20,000 m (50 m/min, 90 min set-up, 10 points losses) raises capacity from 42,455 m to about:
questions.explain: 400 ÷ 490 = 81.6%; net 71.6%; 72,000 × 0.716 = 51,575 m. Capacity does not double because the run was already most of the clock time.

questions.q: Net efficiency can never be higher than calculated efficiency.
questions.explain: Net efficiency = calculated efficiency − miscellaneous losses, and losses are never negative.

questions.q: Dyeing and printing capacity per day: continuous 34,000 + batch 10,000 + stenter-dyed 34,000 + printing 48,185. Total metres per day?
questions.explain: 34,000 + 10,000 + 34,000 + 48,185 = 126,185 m, the "about 126,000 m" at which the plant is balanced.

questions.q: If 50% of thermosol fabric needs a double pass instead of 25%, the adjusted capacity (from 42,455 m) becomes about:
questions.explain: 42,455 ÷ (1 + 0.50) = 28,303 m. Halving (21,228 m) would be right only if all fabric passed twice.

questions.q: Mercerizing runs at 50 m/min at 80% efficiency. If 60% of the plant's fabric is mercerized, what plant output per day does one mercerizer support?
questions.explain: Machine capacity 57,600 m; ÷ 0.60 = 96,000 m, now below the 126,000 m plant balance, so mercerizing would become a bottleneck.

questions.q: A student computes net efficiency as 69% × 90% = 62.1% instead of 69% − 10% = 59%. For the 72,000 m/day thermosol range the error:
questions.explain: 72,000 × 0.621 = 44,712 m against 42,455 m: about 2,257 m a day too much, which would be promised to buyers and never produced.

questions.q: Finishing capacity is given as 34,000 + 92,160. What is the 34,000 m?
options: Stenter-dyed fabric, which is finished as it is dyed
questions.explain: The stenter-dyeing range (34,000 m after double passes) dries and sets its fabric in the same pass, so it adds to finishing capacity alongside the 92,160 m of the two finishing stenters.

questions.q: A 10,000 m run at 70 m/min with 70 min of set-up. Calculated efficiency in %, to one decimal?

For 10,000 m runs, the pad steam range (70 m/min, 70 min set-up) has a lower net efficiency than the thermosol range (50 m/min, 90 min set-up), because its faster speed makes the run shorter and the set-up a larger share.
questions.explain: Pad steam: 142.9 ÷ 212.9 = 67.1% → 57.1% net. Thermosol: 200 ÷ 290 = 69.0% → 59.0% net. Faster running still gives more metres a day (57,571 vs 42,455), but a lower efficiency.
